cards.title: Introduction to Generics
cards.content:
Introduced in Java 5, Generics enable types (classes and interfaces) to be parameters when defining classes, interfaces, and methods.

Before generics, collections stored raw Object references, requiring explicit type casting and risking runtime exceptions:

// Pre-Java 5
List list = new ArrayList();
list.add("Java");
String s = (String) list.get(0); // Explicit cast needed

With Generics, type casting is eliminated, and errors are caught at compile-time:

// Post-Java 5
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add("Java");
String s = list.get(0); // No cast needed!

options.text: They caused syntax compilation errors whenever any object was added to a List.
They forced runtime Type Casting checks, risking ClassCastExceptions at runtime instead of compile-time.
They prevented the JVM from running garbage collection on collections.
They did not allow storing custom objects inside the ArrayList collections.

cards.title: Generic Classes
cards.content:
A generic class is defined with a type parameter section delimited by angle brackets (<T>) following the class name.

public class Box<T> {
    private T content;

    public void set(T content) {
        this.content = content;
    }

    public T get() {
        return content;
    }
}

Commonly used type parameter names are:

  • E - Element (used extensively by the Java Collections Framework)
  • K - Key
  • V - Value
  • T - Type

cards.title: Generic Methods
cards.content:
Generic methods introduce their own type parameters. The scope of the type parameter is limited to the method where it is declared.

The type parameter section must appear before the method's return type:

public class Utility {
    // Generic method declaration
    public static <K, V> boolean compare(Pair<K, V> p1, Pair<K, V> p2) {
        return p1.getKey().equals(p2.getKey()) && 
               p1.getValue().equals(p2.getValue());
    }
}

To call this method, specify the type arguments explicitly or let the Java compiler infer them:

boolean same = Utility.<Integer, String>compare(p1, p2); // Explicit
boolean sameInferred = Utility.compare(p1, p2);           // Inferred

cards.title: Bounded Type Parameters
cards.content:
Sometimes you need to restrict the kinds of types allowed as arguments. For example, a method operating on numbers might only want to accept instances of Number or its subclasses.

To declare a bounded type parameter, list the type parameter's name, followed by the extends keyword, and then its upper bound:

public class Calculator<T extends Number> {
    private T value;
    
    public double doubleValue() {
        return value.doubleValue(); // Safe to call Number methods!
    }
}

You can also define multiple bounds: <T extends ClassA & InterfaceB>. In this case, ClassA must be declared first.

cards.title: Wildcards & PECS Principle
cards.content:
In generics, wildcards represented by the question mark (?) represent an unknown type.

  • Upper Bounded Wildcards: List<? extends Number>. Allows reading elements safely as Number, but prevents writing elements (except null).
  • Lower Bounded Wildcards: List<? super Integer>. Allows writing elements of type Integer safely, but reading yields only Object.

Remember the PECS guideline:

Producer Extends, Consumer Super

If your generic collection produces data (you only read from it), use ? extends. If it consumes data (you write to it), use ? super.

pairs.target: Producer: Read elements as Numbers; cannot write elements.
Consumer: Write Integers safely; read elements only as Object.
Unbounded: Read elements only as Object; cannot write elements.
Invariant: Must match the exact List containing raw Number objects.

cards.title: Type Erasure
cards.content:
Generics were added to Java without breaking backwards compatibility with older versions. To achieve this, the compiler uses a process called Type Erasure.

During Type Erasure, the compiler:

  • Replaces all type parameters in generic types with their bounds (e.g., Object if unbounded, or Number for extends Number).
  • Inserts explicit type casts where necessary to ensure type safety.
  • Generates synthetic methods (bridge methods) to preserve polymorphism in extended generic types.

Because of this, generic type information is not available at runtime. For example, List<String> and List<Integer> both become the raw type List in byte code.

options.text: You can check generic types at runtime using 'instanceof List<String>'.
The JVM creates a separate compiled class file for every generic type argument used.
At runtime, 'new ArrayList<String>().getClass()' returns the exact same Class object as 'new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass()' due to type erasure.
Array creation of generic types (e.g., 'new T[10]') is highly encouraged and safe.

content.text: During type erasure, to preserve polymorphism and inheritance behaviors on generic overriding methods, the Java compiler automatically generates a synthetic method called a [[blank1]] method.
